title: The Essence of Hayao Miyazaki Films: A Short Documentary About the Humanity at the Heart of His Animation
description:
in Animation, Creativity, Writing |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Film­mak­er Hayao Miyaza­ki detests being referred to as the Japan
body:
in Animation, Creativity, Writing |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Film­mak­er Hayao Miyaza­ki detests being referred to as the Japan­ese Walt Dis­ney. The great ani­ma­tor and sto­ry­teller admires the gor­geous ani­ma­tion of clas­sic Dis­ney films, but finds them lack­ing in emo­tion­al com­plex­i­ty, the ele­ment he prizes above all else.
Miyaza­k­i’s films are cel­e­brat­ed for their mys­ti­cal, super­nat­ur­al ele­ments, but they take shape around the human char­ac­ters inhab­it­ing them. Plot comes lat­er, after he has fig­ured out the desires dri­ving his peo­ple. “Keep it sim­ple,” he coun­sels in Lewis Bond’s short doc­u­men­tary The Essence of Human­i­ty above. An inter­est­ing piece of advice, giv­en that a hall­mark of his 60-year career is his insis­tence on cre­at­ing real­is­tic three-dimen­sion­al char­ac­ters, warts and all.
Amer­i­can ani­ma­tors are also taught to sim­pli­fy. They should all be able to sum up the essence of their pro­posed fea­tures by fill­ing in the blank of the phrase “I want _____,” pre­sum­ably because such con­ci­sion is a nec­es­sary ele­ment of a suc­cess­ful ele­va­tor pitch.
As Bond points out, West­ern ani­mat­ed fea­tures often end with a con­ve­nient deus ex machi­na, free­ing the char­ac­ters up for a crowd-pleas­ing dance par­ty as the cred­its roll.
Miyaza­ki doesn’t cot­ton to the idea of tidy, unearned end­ings, nor does he feel bound to grant his char­ac­ters their wants, pre­fer­ring instead to give them what they need. Spir­i­tu­al growth is supe­ri­or to wish ful­fill­ment here.
Such growth rarely hap­pens with­out time for reflec­tion, and Miyaza­ki films are notable for the num­ber of non-ver­bal scenes where­in char­ac­ters per­form small, every­day actions, a num­ber of which can be sam­pled in Bond’s doc­u­men­tary. The beau­ti­ful­ly ren­dered weath­er and set­tings have pro­vid­ed clues as to the char­ac­ters’ devel­op­ment, ever since the love­ly scene of cloud shad­ows skim­ming across a field in his first fea­ture, 1979’s The Cas­tle of Cagliostro.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.

Ayun Hal­l­i­day is an author, illus­tra­tor, and the­ater mak­er in NYC.

title: Christopher Nolan Picks 15 Favorite Films from the Criterion Closet
description:
in Film |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Maybe you’ve already seen Christo­pher Nolan’s new cin­e­mat­ic inter­pre­ta­tion of the Ody
body:
in Film |   	July 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Maybe you’ve already seen Christo­pher Nolan’s new cin­e­mat­ic inter­pre­ta­tion of the Odyssey more than once; maybe you don’t know whether you’ll ever get around to it at all. Either way, you’ve got to admit that the man makes films in a way very few liv­ing direc­tors do. His com­bi­na­tion of block­buster-scale spec­ta­cle and per­son­al vision, a rare expe­ri­ence indeed at the the­ater these days, can real­ly only be achieved by film­mak­ers with a thor­ough­go­ing love of the medi­um. Most of us will require no fur­ther proof of that love than this new video cap­tur­ing his vis­it to the Cri­te­ri­on Clos­et, that both hal­lowed and much-YouTubed space jam-packed with releas­es from the most wide­ly known home-video brand for cinephiles.
Unsur­pris­ing­ly, it’s not his first vis­it. “Last time I was here, there were no cam­eras, and I got to just come and steal some films,” he says, “but now I’m singing for my sup­per.” Unlike some film­mak­ers, he does­n’t play it cool for the audi­ence; rather, he imme­di­ate­ly starts pulling down Don Siegel’s neo-noir Hem­ing­way adap­ta­tion The Killers, a five-pic­ture John Cas­savetes box set, and Al Rein­ert’s Bri­an Eno-scored NASA doc­u­men­tary For All Mankind. It’s not a sur­prise to see him go for an Orson Welles movie, but the one that first catch­es his eye is Mr. Arkadin, which Welles “made all over the world in the scrap­pi­est, most sort of home­made, put-his-friends-togeth­er, grab-some-cos­tumes, find-an-inter­est­ing-loca­tion kind of way.”
Fritz Lang’s The Tes­ta­ment of Dr. Mabuse, he recalls, pro­vid­ed him and his broth­er-col­lab­o­ra­tor inspi­ra­tion for the Jok­er as famous­ly por­trayed by Heath Ledger in The Dark Knight. The com­plete Apu tril­o­gy by Satya­jit Ray reminds him that, how­ev­er great an impact the first of those films made on him, he nev­er did watch the oth­er two. For many movie­go­ers in the Eng­lish-speak­ing world of the mid-twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry, Ray’s work was some of the first “world cin­e­ma” they’d ever seen; Nolan’s fel­low cinephile-auteur Mar­tin Scors­ese has done his part to bol­ster that tra­di­tion with his World Cin­e­ma Project series, and Nolan pulls off the shelf one of its vol­umes fea­tur­ing pic­tures from Cuba, Indone­sia, Iran, and else­where.
Though tech­ni­cal­ly British, Nolan is the par­tial­ly Chica­go-raised son of an Amer­i­can moth­er long since accept­ed as a kind of Hol­ly­wood native. His taste in movies, too, reflects a streak of high Amer­i­can­ism, which man­i­fests in selec­tions like Spike Lee’s Mal­colm X, David Lynch’s Lost High­way, Carl Franklin’s One False Move, and Richard Lin­klater’s Boy­hood. (As for Robert Alt­man’s satir­i­cal thriller The Play­er, it would be hard to imag­ine how he could­n’t appre­ci­ate its wicked­ly inci­sive depic­tion of “the Indus­try.”) Com­ing to the end of his Clos­et time, he also man­ages to grab God­frey Reg­gio’s Qat­si tril­o­gy, which con­sti­tutes “one of the great pieces of pure cin­e­ma,” and Car­roll Bal­lard’s The Black Stal­lion, a child­hood favorite that stayed with him. Like all the most suc­cess­ful film­mak­ers, Nolan under­stands that you’ve got to end strong, and in a way that does­n’t require expla­na­tion: hence, per­haps, his final choice of Cit­i­zen Kane.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: A Guerrilla Girl Drops Her Mask
description:

body:
Daily Newsletter
                Joyce Kozloff becomes the first public member of the feminist collective. Also: Why is an AI company stamping its name onto an art school?
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Four decades ago, the Guerrilla Girls changed the museum landscape for good. The collective has fought against sexism and racism in the art world ever since, all while keeping their identities anonymous — until now. Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar reports on artist Joyce Kozloff’s decision to reveal her role as a founding Guerrilla Girl last week.Also in the news, a MAGA-friendly artist’s sculpture of Thomas Jefferson is the latest addition to the Rose Garden, part of Trump’s plan to restructure the White House grounds. Further down the rabbit hole of technocracy, AI company Nvidia has stamped its CEO’s name onto the next iteration of San Francisco’s California College of the Arts, which will reopen as a satellite campus of Vanderbilt University.Elsewhere in the Bay Area, another vision of art and political engagement blooms in the work of Emory Douglas, former Black Panther Party culture minister. Critic Max Blue visits the 83-year-old artist’s survey exhibition for a bracing reminder that art can be a portal to a better world.—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

	
		
			Joyce Kozloff Reveals Herself as Guerrilla Girls Founding Member
		
	
	
		Artist and activist Joyce Kozloff has taken off the mask after 41 years, disclosing in a new interview with Art Journal Open that she was among the founding members of the Guerrilla Girls.

She also revealed that “Liubov Popova” was her assigned pseudonym within the collective, whose members took the names of late women artists to maintain their own anonymity. In 2016, she published a (sneaky) biographical essay in Hyperallergic that both examined and lauded the Russian artist’s creative evolution and career milestones throughout her unfortunately short life. | Rhea Nayyar
	
	
		Read More

title: Archie Rand’s Landmark Letter Paintings Acquired by Italy’s Modena FC Collection
description: For decades, Archie Rand‘s “Letter Paintings” series has been something of a cult favorite among painters and critics. Now, 44 of them are heading t
body:
For decades, Archie Rand‘s “Letter Paintings” series has been something of a cult favorite among painters and critics. Now, 44 of them are heading to an unlikely home: the corporate collection of Italy’s Modena FC.

	New York–based gallery Jarvis Art announced this week that the Italian football club has acquired the group of paintings, which Rand made between 1968 and 1971 while still a teenager. The series was shown in 1983 at the Museum of the Carnegie Institute and reunited in a 1991 exhibition at Exit Art in New York, where it earned a jazzy review from New York Times critic Roberta Smith. The works have rarely been seen together since.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The paintings marked an early turning point for Rand. As a teenager, he apprenticed under painter Larry Poons and became an acolyte of the influential critic Clement Greenberg, who saw the young artist as part of the next generation of abstract painters. But instead of following that path to its logical conclusion, Rand veered off script. He began writing the names of the musicians, poets, artists, and public figures he loved across luminous abstract canvases, turning Color Field painting into something deeply personal.


			
			
			
	
			
					Archie Rand, LaVern Baker, 1969.
	



	Looking back years later, Rand described the works as “tombstones for the unheralded.” They were, he said, an attempt to paint something modern art had largely forgotten: love.

	In her review, Smith argued the paintings deserved far more attention than they had received. She praised the way they fused the lush surfaces of Color Field painting with the language and references of Conceptual art, calling them works that balanced “reverence and irreverence.” She went on to suggest they anticipated later developments ranging from New Image Painting to Jean-Michel Basquiat’s use of musicians’ names.

	“This acquisition of one of Archie’s most prominent historical series, along with the great success of his recent show at the gallery, Heads, is a testament to the longevity of his work, not just today but throughout his career,” said Lindsay Jarvis, founder of Jarvis Art.

title: Thieves Snatch 2,500-Year-Old Celtic Gold Torque from French Museum in Broad Daylight
description: A 2,500-year-old gold collar belonging to the Vix Treasure archaeological find was stolen Friday in broad daylight from a French museum, according t
body:
A 2,500-year-old gold collar belonging to the Vix Treasure archaeological find was stolen Friday in broad daylight from a French museum, according to reports in Le Parisien and France 3.

	The thieves allegedly entered the Musée du Pays Châtillonnais – Trésor de Vix in Châtillon-sur-Seine, Burgundy, around 10:30 a.m. on July 24 by paying the admission fee, acting as regular visitors to the museum. Dijon prosecutor Olivier Caracotch said in a statement to Le Parisien that the thieves smashed the display case holding the gold collar, called a torque, before fleeing the museum through the main entrance.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Caracotch added that his office has opened an investigation for organized crime and that the Juridiction interrégionale spécialisée (JIRS) in Nancy will assist “given this classification, the nature of the facts, and the great complexity of the procedure.”  

	Jérémie Brigand, the mayor of Châtillon-sur-Seine and president of Communauté de Communes du Pays Châtillonnais, said in a statement, according to Le Parisien, that the museum had faced “two previous failed nighttime burglary attempts” in the past eight months. The museum said that it had upped its security as a result, spending some €150,000 ($171,000) on new security cameras, motion detectors, and door detectors, per the France 3 report.

	 “Despite these measures, the perpetrators demonstrated an organization, a speed of execution and a determination that allowed them to carry out their action,” he said in his Le Parisien statement, characterizing the theft as an “attack on cultural heritage and the public interest.”

	He told France 3 that the stolen torque is “priceless, it’s a unique piece in the world. And beyond the value of the gold, it’s a historical piece of Châtillonnais heritage. And it’s really damaging and regrettable that criminals are attacking the history of the Châtillonnais and our country.”

	The torque theft recalls the brazen theft at the Louvre in Paris, in which thieves made off with $102 million worth of jewels in less than eight minutes, also in broad daylight. That high-profile theft ultimately caused the museum’s president to resign and expedited the Louvre’s plans to address its dated security systems, which the museum is expected to begin in January 2027. The Louvre’s Apollo Gallery, where the stolen crown jewels had been on display, reopened this week without the jewels, which are still missing.
	

	The Louvre heist led to several other museums across France facing similar thefts. Earlier this month, thieves targeted another French museum, stealing some $4.57 million worth of jewels from the Lalique Museum in Wingen-sur-Moder, Alsace.

	The Vix Treasure was discovered in 1953 at the foot of Mont Lassois, near the village of Vix, or about 4 miles north of Châtillon-sur-Seine, where the museum is located, according to its website. The heart of the findings was the tomb of a woman, called the “Dame of Vix” (Princess of Vix), who is believed to have been buried between 470 and 460 BCE.

	The tomb was filled with precious objects, including the golden torque, which is made of 24-karat gold, weighs just over a pound, and dates to the 6th century BCE; the Vix Krater, which includes a depiction of Medusa and was produced around 530 BCE in the Greek colony of Sybaris in southern Italy and it is unknown how it came to Vix; and the Silver Phiale, likely a ceremonial item that is the “oldest silver vase discovered north of the Alps.”  

	The golden torque is of a Celtic design in the shape of an arc “with its two ends resting on a lion paw that is positioned on hollow spheres,” per the museum, which notes that it was a symbol of power. Atop each lion paw is a depiction of the winged horse Pegasus, representing the Greek influence on the region during the era. That influence is juxtaposed with Celtic imagery of “two pear-shaped balls [that] symbolize the sun.”  
	

	Initially, the torque was discovered on the princess’s skull and believed to be a diadem, but further research confirmed that it was “worn around the neck, like a necklace, by a member of the aristocracy. Its placement in the tomb likely resulted from the tomb’s collapse shortly after the burial,” per the museum.  

	The museum adds, “Through its iconographic elements and method of manufacture, the torque reflects a blend of cultures and a transfer of technology, illustrating the vibrant trade in Europe at the end of the First Iron Age.”
